en: We are Geyer's black bands, heia oho!
And want to brawl with tyrants, heia oho!
Spears forward, at them and on,
set the red cock on the monastery roof.
We want to complain to the Lord in heaven, kyrieleys,
that we may not beat the priests to death, kyrieleys.
Spears forward, …
When Adam dug and Eve span, kyrieleys,
where then was the nobleman? kyrieleys.
Spears forward, …
Now it is the turn of castle, abbey and chapter, heia oho!
nothing counts for us but the holy Scripture, heia oho!
Spears forward, …
Florian Geyer leads us, in spite of outlawry and excommunication.
He bears the Bundschuh on his banner, has helmet and armour on.
Spears forward, …
At Weinsberg there was fire and stench, heia oho!
Many a man jumped over the blade, heia oho!
Spears forward, …
The nobleman's little daughter, heia oho!
we sent her off into hell, heia oho!
Spears forward, …
Beaten, we march home, heia oho!
our grandchildren will fight it out better, heia oho!
Spears forward, …
notes: 'heia oho' and 'kyrieleys' are kept as sung: 'heia oho' is a wordless cry; 'kyrieleys' is a shortened 'Kyrie eleison' ('Lord, have mercy'), the refrain of old German pilgrims' and soldiers' songs.

'Spieß voran, drauf und dran' is translated plainly: 'Spieß' is the pike or spear, 'voran' forward, 'drauf und dran' onto them and at them. The source abbreviates the refrain after the first stanza ('Spieß voran, …'); kept so.

line 1.1: Florian Geyer (c. 1490–1525), a Franconian knight who led a peasant troop in the Peasants' War; 'Geyer' is kept as a name (it also means 'vulture'). 'Haufen' = a band or troop (the word for a fighting company of the time); the black band is his troop.
line 1.4: 'den roten Hahn aufs Dach setzen' (to put the red cock on the roof) is an idiom for setting a building on fire.
line 2.2: 'könnten' is read as a lament that they may not (are not allowed to) kill the priests; it can also be read 'that we could kill the priests'. 'Pfaffen' is a contemptuous word for clergy.
line 3.1-2: the old saying of the English Peasants' Revolt, 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?', in German.
line 4.1: 'Jetzt gilt es ...' = now it is aimed at, now it is the turn of; 'Stift' = a collegiate church or religious foundation (chapter).
line 5.1: 'Acht und Bann' = the imperial ban (outlawry) and the Church's ban (excommunication).
line 5.2: 'Bundschuh' = the laced peasant shoe, the emblem of the peasant risings, kept as a name.
line 6.1: Weinsberg, a town stormed in the Peasants' War; 'setzt es Brand und Stank' = there came (literally 'it set') fire and stench.
line 6.2: 'über die Klinge springen' (to jump over the blade) is an idiom for being put to the sword, killed.
line 7.2: 'in die Höll' hinein schicken' = to send into hell, i.e. to kill.
